title: The disease of envy
hook: envy eats good deeds as fire eats wood (Abu Dawud)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kibr, arrogance, and your line: reject pride, not truth. Did a correction come, and did you manage a you're right? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

Dry wood in a fire doesn't get a little smaller. It goes. Log, flame, ash. A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud borrows that picture: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported to have warned against envy, because it eats up good deeds the way fire eats wood. Not dents them. Eats them. Which is a strange thought, because envy doesn't do anything to anyone. It's a feeling about someone else's life, scrolling past, sitting quietly. And yet in this hadith it burns the envier's own woodpile. Today's word: hasad, envy.
screen: `DRY WOOD IN A FIRE.` → `IT EATS GOOD DEEDS.` → `HASAD.`

segments.voice: Start where the Qur'an starts. A short surah near its end, al-Falaq, is a request for refuge, and one of the things it asks refuge from is this, in Pickthall's words: "And from the evil of the envier when he envieth." Envy is serious enough to need protecting from. Now the careful part. Scholars draw a line between two wishes. Hasad is wishing that someone's blessing were taken away from them. The other wish is to have the same good too, without wanting it gone from them, and scholars call that ghibtah. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even uses the word envy for that second kind: there's no envy, it says, except toward a person given wealth who spends it rightly, and a person given wisdom who judges by it and teaches it. So wanting to be like someone good isn't the disease. Wanting them brought down is. Then the Qur'an goes one level earlier, to the wanting itself: "And covet not the thing in which Allah hath made some of you excel others." And last, the cure in today's line. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a Muslim prays for a brother who isn't there, an angel answers: and for you the same. So the prayer for the person you envy turns around and lands on you. Fire eats wood. A prayer for them adds to the pile.
screen: `REFUGE FROM THE ENVIER.` · `WANTING IT GONE, OR WANTING IT TOO.` · `COVET NOT.` · then, large: `AND FOR YOU THE SAME.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for someone you envy. Settle, and breathe. Let one name come up. The friend with the easy job, the cousin with the house, the stranger online whose life looks finished and framed. Notice the tightness the name brings, and don't argue with it. Now turn toward them. If you pray, you can ask, in your own words, that their good thing stay with them and grow. If you don't, simply hold the wish that it go well for them. Keep the name, drop the comparison. The bell holds the time.
Hasad. Envy; wishing someone's blessing were taken from them. Wanting the same good without wanting it gone is called ghibtah. Today's word.

Your line: pray for them. Today, the next time someone's good news stings, say a good word for them, out loud or under your breath. Tomorrow, the disease that hides inside good deeds: showing off. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims seek refuge from envy in Surah al-Falaq, and teachers distinguish hasad, wishing a blessing gone, from ghibtah, wishing for the same good; praying for the person one envies is a remedy often taught.

myth: the hadith says envy eats good deeds as fire eats wood
the picture is from Sunan Abu Dawud: log, flame, ash.
any wish to have what someone else has is hasad
wanting the same good without wanting it taken from them is what scholars call ghibtah.
al-Falaq asks refuge from the envier
"And from the evil of the envier when he envieth."

fork.setup: a colleague gets the promotion you wanted. by today's teaching, which wish is hasad?
options: I wish I had one like it.
I wish she didn't have it.
I hope it goes well for her.
fork.reveal: hasad is wishing the blessing gone. wanting the same is ghibtah, and the third is the cure: a prayer for her, which, in the hadith, an angel answers for you too.

original.note: Arabic: envy, wishing another's blessing were removed.

trapdoor: what you thought: envy is a private feeling that hurts nobody.
what it means: in the hadith it eats the envier's own good deeds, as fire eats wood.
what a scholar hears: the distinction between hasad and ghibtah, the hadith of the two people it's allowed to envy, and the angel's 'and for you the same.'
